title: Ford unveils the GT41 as it hopes to win Le Mans again
author: Jonathan M. Gitlin
body: Sixty years ago, after two failed attempts, Ford won the 24 Hours of Le Mans with its GT40 race car. In the years since, the Blue Oval has been back to France more than a few times, with varying success. It could never replicate the GT40’s success winning overall, but it celebrated the 40th anniversary with a class win . Now it wants another shot at the really big trophy , and it debuted the car during the Detroit Lions-Chicago Bears football game today: meet the GT41. “Revealing the Ford GT41 is a significant moment for everyone involved in this program,” said Dan Sayers, manager of Ford Racing’s Hypercar program. “It's the result of an enormous amount of work across our engineering, design, and development teams and an important milestone on our journey towards 2027. We know the scale of the challenge ahead—the level of competition in Hypercar is incredibly high, and there are no shortcuts to success. Our focus has been on building the right foundations, bringing together the right people and making sure we learn as much as possible from every stage of development.” The video was directed by Zack Snyder and features Matt Damon’s voice-over. Like many other entrants in the World Endurance Championship’s Hypercar class, Ford has chosen the rear-wheel-drive LMDh technical approach rather than building the GT41 entirely from scratch, as Ferrari and Aston Martin do with their cars. LMDh cars start with one of four approved carbon fiber chassis—in this case, Ford is working with Oreca, which has also partnered with Genesis and Acura. Read full article Comments

body: Elon Musk's social network X just got a new feature it never had under previous ownership. That would be parental controls for teen users, to be exact. In a new post from the official Safety account on X, the company announced it has implemented parental controls for users aged 13 to 17. The way it works is that an account run by a parent or guardian establishes a supervisory link to the account run by a teen, which gives the parent or guardian access to a bunch of monitoring and safety features the site didn't have before. These features include the ability to monitor usage and set daily limits for the teen, as well as the option to require new followers to be approved by the parent or guardian. Recommendations on the For You feed can be limited to accounts the teen already follows, while parents can mute specific words, control who can send direct messages, and see who the teens have chatted with in DMs without seeing the messages themselves. title: Anthropics Claude now lets you turn artifacts into apps
body: So you asked Claude to help you remember when to take out the trash, and it ridiculously over-engineered it and created a beautiful interactive artifact with timelines, graphs, and a calendar? Well, now that you've gotten that far, why not turn the artifact into a full-fledged app on your desktop? A new update to Anthropic's Claude allows you to do exactly that, though there are some limitations. Artifacts, if you aren't familiar with Claude, are work outputs that are similar to webpages, and they can contain charts, graphs, text, photos, videos, and interactive elements, but until now they only lived inside Claude. Now, when you open an artifact in Claude, you can click on the drop-down menu on the top left and select "Install as an app." Besides being more convenient, since they live on your desktop, these apps can perform actions such as sending notifications or adding items to your menu bar. Of course, you can set permissions for apps to make sure they don't overstep their boundaries; by default, they can only do what they'd be able to do in a browser, but you can go as far as to give them full access to your computer. I've tried this out on my Mac, and it worked well, though I couldn't install all my artifacts as apps. Anthropic says some artifacts can't be installed as apps, which includes Claude Docs, Slides, and Sheets. The ability to install artifacts as apps is rolling out to all plans as a beta feature. title: Draining peatlands is responsible for a few percent of our global warming
author: Scott K. Johnson
body: Much of the focus for human-caused climate change is on fossil fuels, which are creating most of our problems. But land use change is also a large component of the story, accounting for about one-third of total historical CO 2 emissions. Deforestation plays a major role here, but practices like draining wetlands also factor in. Exactly how much of our history of eliminating wetlands has contributed to warming is challenging to figure out. But thanks to new sources of data that measure emissions from today’s surviving wetlands, it’s possible to put a better number on it. A new study led by Jevan Yu at MIT focuses on peatlands—environments like bogs and fens where organic matter accumulates into thick layers of material. Some 600 billion tons of carbon are held in these vast stores of peat, which is more than you can find in all the world’s living vegetation, the researchers note. Because these areas are permanently inundated, any oxygen in the water is quickly used up, leaving the job of decaying all that organic matter to anaerobic bacteria that work much more slowly and don't digest everything. So instead of seeing organic carbon turning into the CO 2 gas released by aerobic bacteria, in peatlands, a subset of it gradually turns into methane gas. Methane is an even more potent greenhouse gas than CO 2 itself and ultimately gets oxidized into CO 2 . That means there’s a little trade-off from peatlands—most of the carbon they have is kept out of the atmosphere, but the carbon that does escape does so as methane. Read full article Comments

The comedian and Crazy Ex-Girlfriend creator has uploaded her poignant, smart, hilarious, 77-minute, one-woman comedy special Death, Let Me Do My Special to YouTube. body: Talking dolls and stuffed animals have been holiday gifts for decades. But with the rapid adoption of AI across all industries, many of the toys on shelves today can answer questions , make up stories, and carry on full conversations with a child. In New York, those toys have a few more months on the shelves. On Tuesday, Nov. 24, New York Gov. Kathy Hochul signed a law banning the manufacture, distribution, and sale of children s toys with built-in AI companions in the state for five years. The ban takes effect Feb. 22, 2027, though, so the toys can still be sold over the holidays. Hochul urged parents to think twice before buying an AI toy this holiday season. "Parents shopping for gifts for the holidays or any other occasion should not have to worry that dangerous chatbots disguised as toys could expose their children to inappropriate conversations, manipulate their feelings or put their privacy at risk," she said in a statement. title: European spacecraft finds chaotic scene after asteroid deflection experiment
author: Stephen Clark
body: Four years ago, NASA dispatched a small spacecraft on a suicide mission to show how humanity might deflect an asteroid on a collision course with Earth. The first-of-its-kind experiment worked beautifully as the solar-powered space probe slammed into asteroid Dimorphos, permanently altering its trajectory. Using telescopes, astronomers measured changes in the orbit of Dimorphos around a larger asteroid companion named Didymos in the aftermath of NASA's Double Asteroid Redirection Test (DART) mission. The spacecraft released some 10 billion joules of energy as it impacted Dimorphos in September 2022 at more than 13,700 mph (6.14 kilometers per second), shortening the asteroid's 12-hour orbit around Didymos by about 33 minutes, 25 times the most conservative expectation. But scientists could only learn so much from DART. The collision destroyed the spacecraft, as expected. DART recorded images as it took aim on Dimorphos, but only faraway telescopes and a small CubeSat that briefly detected the impact flash could see what happened next. Read full article Comments

title: Study: Meta settlement needs YouTube, TikTok to succeed
body: When Meta settled a massive social media addiction lawsuit brought by multiple state attorneys general in August, it invited YouTube and TikTok to join the terms. Meta, which agreed to implement new restrictions on teen use , argued that the safeguards amounted to a new industry standard. They included a two-hour daily time limit, removing nighttime access to Meta apps by default, and no notifications during school hours. "These protections will only be truly effective if we work with our peers TikTok and YouTube to put the same measures in place," Meta said in a statement at the time. Neither social media platform has joined the settlement since. SEE ALSO: 5 of the biggest changes coming to Instagram, Facebook Now, a new study published in JAMA suggests Meta was right about the potential effect of YouTube and TikTok agreeing to the restrictions. The authors analyzed existing data from ongoing research known as the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development (ABCD) Study, which tracks teen screen time and social media habits. They looked at data from 1,803 participants over a five-year period between Nov. 2020 and Aug. 2025. They found the Meta apps Instagram and Facebook accounted for only 20 percent of total daily social media use amongst those participants. Snapchat, TikTok, and YouTube comprised the remaining apps named in the litigation. Additionally, the authors found that significantly more teens would benefit from the time limit, nighttime access, and notification restrictions if the other companies implemented them. title: Can AI make Thanksgiving less painful?
body: I have a liberal friend who I was talking with the other day about plans for Thanksgiving. He s going home to his family in Oklahoma, who are anything but liberal. "I m dreading it," he said. "My uncle sits in a chair watching Fox News on his phone, and my great-aunt will try to tell me in so many ways, without telling me, that I m going to hell for being gay." Every November, we all pretend that turkey, stuffing, and pumpkin pie are worth being trapped by three generations of relatives you barely know. Just call me the Grinch of Thanksgiving. Sure, not all of us are in an inhospitable environment like that, but for many, it's as awkward as waving back at someone on the street who was actually waving at the person behind you. When the atmosphere is heavy, with everyone waiting for the proverbial shoe to drop, it inevitably does loudly, like a construction boot. Years ago, with a former partner s parents, the mother dropped her fork, pointed across the table at me, and said in Spanish, "I can t look at him." It was all downhill from there. Tech breaking the ice? Back in the day, before technology swallowed us whole and gave us hunched necks, surviving Thanksgiving required biting your tongue, heavy drinking though that often fueled the fires of ferocity or staying away. Your only defenses were hiding in the bathroom, taking a long nap, or pretending to be a die-hard Detroit Lions fan (they traditionally play every Thanksgiving), eyes and ears glued to the TV to tune out the bickering. title: FCC clears SpaceX to put up to 1 million AI satellites in orbit
body: An AI chatbot may be able to answer a question in seconds, but the chips doing the work need a steady supply of electricity and a way to get rid of all the heat they generate. SpaceX wants to put some of those chips on satellites and power them with sunlight. In outer space. On Wednesday, Nov. 25, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC) gave Elon Musk 's SpaceX conditional approval to deploy up to 1 million satellites for its Starmind project, a network of orbital data centers that would process information for use back on Earth. According to the FCC, it's "the first authorization in U.S. history for a constellation of data centers in space." When could SpaceX launch its AI satellites? SpaceX says the factory it s building in Bastrop, Texas, could start turning out satellites for launch as early as late 2027. The FCC's deadline for the first one is Nov. 25, 2033. By then, SpaceX has to have a Starmind satellite in its assigned orbit and running. Two years later, the FCC expects 100,000 satellites to be operating. That's nearly nine times as many satellites as SpaceX's Starlink network has in orbit today. The next deadlines are 500,000 by Nov. 2038 and the full million by Nov. 2040. Under the terms of the order, missing those deadlines would void the authorization. SpaceX is counting on its Starship rocket to carry the heavy satellites into orbit in large numbers. Amazon Leo, which is building a rival to Starlink, called the proposal a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan" in a March petition. title: Black Friday scams: How to protect yourself as cyberattacks threaten retailers
body: With Black Friday almost upon us, it's time to talk about something other than what you should buy or how much it costs. The biggest shopping day of the year in the United States can also be one of the most precarious, thanks to an increased reliance on e-commerce in the age of rampant cyberattacks and system outages. There's only so much that you, as an individual shopper, can do to protect yourself if an online retailer is compromised or if you're targeted by a scam artist, but it's important to understand those measures regardless. Here are some common-sense things you can do to make sure Black Friday doesn't become a massive headache for you or your family. SEE ALSO: Black Friday TV deals are already live: Get an OLED TV for $799 and save 50% on TCL, LG, and Hisense Don't get phished One of the main ways that bad actors will try to get you during this holiday shopping season is through phishing , which describes a variety of techniques used by scammers to trick people into giving up money or personal information. For example, you may get text messages or emails warning of an urgent problem, such as someone using your card to buy something fraudulently, or something more mundane like a delivery notification. While you don't want to outright ignore these warnings because there is always a slim possibility that they are real, you need to double and triple-check things like the sender's email address or a URL or phone number they've given you to solve the "problem." author: Eric Berger
body: In an extraordinary decision, the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday granted SpaceX conditional authorization to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to serve as orbital data centers. title: The best (and weirdest) Spotify Wrapped features through the years
body: Every year, Spotify Wrapped kicks off the same ritual: Instagram Stories fill up with top-five lists, friends compare how many minutes they spent listening, and someone has to explain how a song they swear they barely played ended up at No. 1. Over the years, Spotify has gotten a lot more creative with those numbers. It's turned listening habits into personality tests , matched people with cities they've never visited, and even stacked their favorite genres into a sandwich . With another Wrapped around the corner, we're looking back at the features that made us laugh, argue with our results, or wonder what exactly Spotify was thinking. Sound Town gave your Spotify habits a hometown (2023) This Tweet is currently unavailable. It might be loading or has been removed. In 2023 , Spotify Wrapped could tell you where in the world people listened to music just like you. The feature, called Sound Town , matched listeners with one of more than 1,300 places, from Provo, Utah, to Cuiab , Brazil, to Burlington, Vermont. To get a match, at least three of your most-played artists had to be especially popular in the same city. The fun was finding out what else people in your Sound Town had on repeat. For example, SZA's "Kill Bill" was No. 1 in both Berkeley, California, and Cambridge, Massachusetts, and came in fifth in Jakarta, Indonesia. In Burlington, Vermont, Noah Kahan had four songs in the top 10. "Stick Season" was No. 1, naturally. title: Ladybird browser's first downloadable alpha is surprisingly capable
author: Nick Indge
body: Note: At the time of writing, I was unaware of criticism directed at Ladybird creator Andreas Kling’s public statements. Readers interested in this background can find further context in accounts by Kelson Vibber and Drew DeVault . After four years of work to build a browser engine from scratch, the Ladybird project released its first downloadable alpha on November 23, offering prebuilt versions for macOS and Linux. Previously, curious users had to compile the browser themselves from its source. Now it's an installable package with automatic updating. Ladybird is most notable for what it isn't: another browser fork. Where Chrome, Edge, Brave, and Opera all run on Google's Blink engine, and Firefox depends on Gecko, Ladybird's rendering engine and its LibJS JavaScript engine were written from scratch. "The engine is our own, built from the ground up, and not a fork," project lead Andreas Kling wrote in Monday's announcement. "The browser around it is modest, but functional." title: Data center emissions are worse than we knew, Harvard study confirms
body: This past election, Americans across the country rejected data centers , voting to restrict new projects in their communities. As voters push back against data centers, a new study out of Harvard reveals startling revelations about the severity of the pollution they create. Pollution from data centers is three times higher than previously estimated, according to a new study from the Harvard Data Science Initiative. The study examined 403 "hyperscale" data centers and found that emissions from these facilities were underestimated. In fact, the lead author Gianluca Guidi believes that their research only provides a "floor estimate." When factoring in the thousands of data centers across the country, many of which were not included in the study, the energy use is likely much higher. SEE ALSO: Is this the only U.S. town to vote 'yes' on data centers? The study found that the largest data centers in the U.S. use as much energy in a single year as the state of Michigan does. Carbon emissions from these data centers surpassed those of entire countries. Researchers found that 2 percent of all electricity use in the U.S. during the study period came from data centers. A single data center included in the study consumed as much energy as 30,000 homes on average. title: Ars Live recap: Don’t expect military attacks on data centers to stop
author: Jeremy Hsu
body: Drone attacks on data centers. Amazon data centers came under military attack for the first time ever in the Middle East this year, and Russia and Ukraine exchanged an unprecedented flurry of drone strikes on each other’s data centers. To examine what such attacks on data centers mean for the future of cloud services that all modern societies depend upon, Ars hosted a live discussion. In a conversation with Ars Technica Tech Reporter Jeremy Hsu, Joseph Jarnecki at the Royal United Services Institute first talked about why public cloud data centers have increasingly become military targets during the 2026 Iran war and the ongoing full-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine: We see an increasing acknowledgement and fact of dual use in particularly the public cloud, but also just across the board in private cloud data centers as well. The dual use that I refer to is the utilization of compute functions within these data centers—within cloud services—by militaries, for example, to run battlefield management systems, to do their HR, to do their resource management. Once a military uses a piece of civilian infrastructure, at least under international law or in terms of the principles of targeting that are taken forward by militaries, it can sometimes become a military object and is therefore of interest to an adversary, and there's an incentive to target it. title: Blade Runner 2099 sneaks in a book detail that never made it into the movies
body: As adaptations go, Blade Runner is a fairly loose take on Philip K. Dick's Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep ? The 1982 film replaces the novel's androids (or "andys") with replicants. Characters from the novel were cut, including Iran, the wife of Rick Deckard (Harrison Ford), and John Isidore, who houses the androids Deckard hunts. (William Sanderson's J.F. Sebastian effectively replaces him in the film.) These are just some world-building details from Dick's work that Blade Runner couldn't fit into a feature-length film. However, one of these missing elements just made its way into the Blade Runner 2099 TV series. SEE ALSO: 'Blade Runner 2099' does what no 'Blade Runner' movie has done before Who is Wilbur Mercer? In Blade Runner 2099 's sixth episode, replicants Julius (Tom Burke) and Clotilde (Amy Lennox) drive past a large billboard that advertises "the power of Mercer." The display is a reference to the fictional religion of Mercerism, built around the martyr Wilbur Mercer. Much of the rest of the episode takes place at the abandoned island Mercer Monastery where Cora (Hunter Schafer) grew up. Mercerism was initially conceptualized in Dick's 1964 short story "The Little Black Box . " Followers connect with Mercer by gripping the handles of an empathy box. This device allows the user to experience Mercer's climb to his death: a slow ascent up a hill during which he's stoned repeatedly. title: Blade Runner 2099 finally takes this franchise to the stars
body: Blade Runner 2099 walks lovingly in the footsteps of Ridley Scott and Denis Villeneuve's preceding Blade Runner films, echoing their memorable cyberpunk settings and noir detective stories. However, there's one area where the TV show completely outpaces both films. SEE ALSO: 'Blade Runner 2099' sneaks in a book detail that never made it into the movies Like Blade Runner and Blade Runner 2049, Blade Runner 2099 takes place primarily in Los Angeles, rarely leaving the city outskirts. Its world is one of bustling streets, crowded apartment buildings, and the massive pyramids that tower over the Los Angeles skyline. Yet episode 2 opens with a different landscape entirely: a fiery red terrain bursting with rocky crags and rushing lava flows. This is Namaka Moon, a real-life satellite of the dwarf planet Haumea. It's also the first time an on-screen Blade Runner project has been to space. (Notably, comic Blade Runner 2019: Off World has already blasted off to space.) Space travel is a fact of life in the world of Blade Runner , as well as in its source material, Philip K. Dick's novel Do Androids Dream of Electric Sheep? As part of larger space colonization attempts, humans are moving to off-world settlements. Who is preparing these settlements for human occupation? Replicants (or androids in the novel), whose enhanced strength and durability make them the ideal slave labor force for braving inhospitable outer space environments. title: Lead azide detonation sends clouds over Iowa as questions of health risks swirl
author: Beth Mole
body: In a powerful explosion that launched gray-white clouds over southeastern Iowa, the Army detonated 68 barrels containing 9,700 pounds (4.4 tons) of degraded lead azide on Wednesday at about 9 am CT, preventing a spontaneous unmitigated explosion of the crystallized, highly unstable compound. The detonation occurred at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa, a town of fewer than 400 people. Residents within a 5-mile area of the facility were advised to evacuate, while people farther out were told to shelter in place, close windows and doors tightly, turn off fans, and set indoor air systems to recirculate. Local Iowa outlet KWQC caught the plume from the two earth-covered containers, which were detonated simultaneously. title: A familiar Iranian hacking group has found a new way to cause chaos
author: Tom Wilson, Financial Times
body: One night in October, hackers staged one of the most unusual cyber attacks in history : cranking up the temperature in refrigeration systems at hundreds of supermarkets across France and destroying millions of euros of food. Hackers have targeted commercial fridges and freezers before, but never at this scale and never in the heart of Europe. The brazen attack left cyber professionals unsure as to who might have executed such a madcap operation. But French intelligence agencies found traces of Farsi and other clues in the digital trail pointing to an elite hacking unit of the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps. The unit allegedly behind the hack, Shahid Kaveh, was already well known to Western intelligence agencies. Named after Mahmoud Kaveh, an Iranian commander who died during the 1980s Iran-Iraq war, it is one of several hacking units overseen by the Revolutionary Guards’ Cyber Electronic Command. title: AI may soon change what it means to be a theoretical physicist
author: Dan Kagan-Kans, Understanding AI
body: About six months ago, Suvrat Raju, a professor of theoretical physics at the International Centre for Theoretical Sciences in Bengaluru, India, asked a frontier AI model to solve a physics problem. He didn’t ask because he needed to know the answer. He had actually solved this particular problem already. But he had never published the solution—which made it a perfect question to test how good AI was at physics. LLMs have been trained on the whole Internet, so if a physics problem has been discussed online, it’s likely the model already knows about it and may have memorized the answer. So a fair test of AI capabilities needs to focus on problems that have never appeared online. The model didn’t answer Raju’s problem correctly, but it did better than he expected—well, enough to get him thinking that the experiment should be repeated and formalized. With the help of a colleague, he set out to create a theoretical physics benchmark for AI. Read full article Comments

title: Centuries-old dust hints at a dying stars last-minute chaos
body: The mix of elements that ends up in planets even people can hinge on a final shake-up inside a dying star , new space observations suggest. A team of researchers studied Cassiopeia A , a glowing cloud of gas and dust left behind by an exploding star. Using NASA 's James Webb Space Telescope , the astronomers could parse out clumps within the 350-year-old cloud and analyze their compositions. The debris from the explosion, called a supernova, is still racing outward in space at about 11 million mph. "What's amazing is that the dust, which we are testing hundreds of years after the explosion, tells us about what happened to the star potentially only hours before it exploded," said Dan Milisavljevic, a Purdue University professor and co-author of the study, in a statement . Supernova explosions forge and scatter many of the heavy elements that later get recycled into new stars and worlds. Computer models have long predicted that a star's inner layers could merge before it explodes. But scientists don't fully understand why and how some stars go through this violent process. The new study , published in The Astrophysical Journal Letters , adds evidence that it happened in Cassiopeia A, giving astronomers a way to peer inside a star that hasn't existed for centuries. Alternatively, what if we just let the franchise rest for a little longer? That seems to be the plan for now, as Lionsgate chairman Adam Fogelson told Variety that there would be no more new films until Collins wrote another book. And honestly, if Collins chooses to move on from Panem forever, would that be so awful? title: Taters and craters: Researchers say potatoes can grow in lunar soil
body: The goal of a self-sustaining lunar colony took a big step forward with the news that potatoes were successfully grown in simulated lunar soil. The tubers were grown by Oregon State University researchers when they "amended" the simulated lunar dirt with organic material. "We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," Aymeric Goyer of Oregon State University s Department of Botany and Plant Pathology said in a press release. "That's an important step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the Moon." With its Artemis missions , NASA is barreling ahead with its plan for a sustained human presence on the Moon. SEE ALSO: Artemis II crew witnessed meteor flashes on the moon with their own eyes Earth's only satellite is covered by a layer of loose rock and dust called regolith, which contains heavy metals and very little organic matter. This makes self-sustaining farming on the Moon difficult. But adding organic matter, called vermicompost, to that lunar regolith can yield potatoes that are both edible and nutritious. Organic matter can be produced by using earthworms to break down food scraps and plant waste. That vermicompost also helps bind the regolith's heavy metals together and makes the soil suitable for producing edible tubers. Researchers tested five different regolith simulants to account for the Moon s varied topsoil. The regolith containing 30 percent vermicompost yielded potatoes that matched those grown on Earth. title: Half of NASA's aging Mars fleet knocked offline by technical issues
author: Stephen Clark
body: Two of NASA's four missions operating at Mars have suspended science operations after encountering separate technical issues in recent weeks. The missions affected by the outages — hopefully temporary — are NASA's Perseverance rover and Odyssey orbiter. Both are operating beyond their original design lifetimes. Perseverance is in its sixth year exploring the surface of Mars, having collected rock and soil samples for eventual return to Earth. The rover is now studying the rim of a crater that once contained an ancient lake of liquid water. Odyssey arrived in orbit around Mars in 2001, and is the longest-lived Mars mission in history. Losing its voice The problem on Perseverance stems from the rover's communications system. The rover has two redundant UHF radios for high-rate communications with a fleet of orbiters that relay data to Earth. A separate X-band system is available for direct-to-Earth communications at a lower data rate. Read full article Comments

title: Unauthorized GTA 6 PC port shut down by Rockstar Games parent company
body: Don't try to port Grand Theft Auto VI to PC yourself or you'll potentially find yourself in big legal trouble. GTA 6 may finally be out on Xbox and PlayStation 5, but that doesn't help out the PC gaming faithful, who still have much longer to wait for their version of the game. As a result, some impatient gamers have recently attempted to create PC ports of the game themselves. Notorious GTA 6 leaker, Cyberleek, also recently released an executable .exe file of the Xbox build of the game, which helped those efforts. Even without Cyberleek, these efforts were probably inevitable, as new AI tools have led to a surge in PS5 jailbreaks and unauthorized ports of classic video games. However, Rockstar Games' parent company, Take-Two Interactive, clearly does not approve of these unofficial attempts to bring GTA 6 to PC ahead of schedule. On Monday, the company had the biggest GTA 6 PC port project, known as Leonida, taken down. So far, GTA 6 has generated billions of dollars, and the PC version could bring in billions more. And when it comes to protecting their IP, Take-Two and Rockstar aren't messing around. GitHub, where the project was hosted, posted a Digital Millennium Copyright Act (DMCA) notice it received from Take-Two. title: Microsoft's historic cloud outage exposed an engineering “fog of war”
author: Nick Indge
body: According to internal memos reviewed by Reuters , Microsoft has declared a "Code Red" overhaul of its engineering response practices after the November 12 outage that lost access to Exchange Online, Teams, and Outlook for users worldwide. Per the memos, Microsoft 365 Core President Jason Henderson described the outage as having the most customer impact in the history of Exchange Online. In a separate memo, Henderson wrote that an urgent production fix in a recent incident took five to six days to reach worldwide saturation. Microsoft's target for its most urgent security fixes is to move from detection to safe worldwide deployment in one hour. "Needless to say, we aren't here yet," Henderson wrote. The memos, which Reuters reviewed but Microsoft has not published, outline the response to the November 12 disruption. The company's post-incident report , dated November 20, attributed the downtime to an undetected Windows scalability defect introduced in July, which caused lock contention in the gateway processes. A Teams traffic failover then dumped additional load onto infrastructure already under stress, as maintenance had left nearly 14 percent of gateway server capacity offline at the time of the incident. title: What's going on with the Riemann hypothesis?
author: John Timmer
body: Last week, news broke that a mathematician had used AI to help crack one of the biggest outstanding problems in math: a proof of the Riemann hypothesis . The news follows several other major breakthroughs in math that have either been enabled by or managed entirely by large language model-based systems, a development that has left the entire field of mathematics in a state of upset. It's too early to say much about the proof itself—mathematicians are still in the process of digesting it. But we can say a little about how the proof came about, and what it tells us about the state of math. Tackling Riemann The Riemann hypothesis dates from the mid-1800s and was formulated by (you will be surprised to learn) Bernhard Riemann. There's not an obvious way to describe the details of the actual hypothesis simply, but it has implications for the distribution of prime numbers. title: Back-to-back measles deaths is our new reality; US tally now at 14
author: Beth Mole
body: Last week, international health authorities formally announced that the US had lost its measles-elimination status, meaning that the virus is once again endemic. But the official determination is a bit like getting the technical readout of a cracked dam while the country is already feet under water. The national tally of measles cases is nearing 6,000 for the year, the highest count since 1991. Transmission is widespread, with 47 states and jurisdictions reporting cases. There have been 43 outbreaks this year, which account for 96 percent of the cases. Four states have case counts above 500, including Pennsylvania, which leads with 1,638 cases as of November 23 . Nearly 650 people have been hospitalized nationwide. As of today, 14 people have died. Deaths and transmission On November 23, Pennsylvania's health department announced its ninth confirmed death, an unvaccinated resident of Centre County. On November 24, Wisconsin reported its third measles death , an adult in Lafayette County. The report follows two other deaths in the state, an infant and a child . New York has also reported a death, which was of a 7-month-old baby . On November 20, Virginia reported the death of a child between the age of 0 and 4 . Read full article Comments

title: How brewers can protect beers from smoke-tainted hops
author: Jennifer Ouellette
body: The 2020 Oregon wildfires burned over 1 million acres, destroyed thousands of structures, and killed 11 people. Smoke from the fires spread across the entire region; this "smoke taint" adversely affected not only local wine production , but also hops grown for beer brewing. Since the Pacific Northwest produces more than 95 percent of US hops and about 40 percent of the global supply, the potential economic impact is significant. That's why Oregon State University (OSU) scientists have been studying how brewers could offset the negative impacts of smoke taint while still incorporating affected hops in their brews. Most recently, they found that it all depends on how much tainted hops are included and when hops are added during the brewing process, according to a new paper published in the Journal of the American Society of Brewing Chemists. As previously reported , the chemistry of brewing beer is a very active area of research. For instance, i n 2018 , OSU chemist Thomas Shellhammer—who also co-authored this latest paper— identified the growing popularity of " dry hopping " (adding hops after fermentation, common for pale ales) among craft brewers as the likely culprit of the exploding beer bottle phenomenon. In a patent application published Nov. 19, the company describes a feature called "My Channel," which would use a viewer's watch history to generate videos for them. In one version, the system could use the viewer's likeness and voice to cast them as the lead of their very own TV show. Patsnap, the database that hosts the filing, offers an AI-generated "technical title" that sums up the idea as a way of "enhancing user engagement." The patent-tracking site Patentlyze first spotted the filing and shared it with 404 Media, which covered it on Nov. 23. Patent records show that Google filed the application on May 13, 2025, but the company has yet to announce a product. What would be on My Channel? One drawing in the application shows a TV menu called "John's Channel," with a crime comedy, a rom-com, a sci-fi adventure, and an action thriller. In a sample prompt, the filing tells the AI to make a video where "the user will play the protagonist." Another example takes that a step further. If a cricket fan has been watching clips about a particular player, the AI could put them in a scene with that player or show them "cheering for India in the stands." title: Tidal announces ban on AI-generated music; 27 million tracks will be deleted
author: Ryan Whitwam
body: Most streaming music providers have opted to label AI-generated content on their platforms, and until now, Tidal was one of them. However, the company is about to take a harder stance. Tidal announced that in the coming weeks, it will fully ban AI music because of the harm it does to human artists. Tidal debuted its initial AI policy in July 2026, which included labeling and demonetizing all songs created entirely with AI. That wasn't enough to stem the tide of AI slop, though. Over the past 90 days, Tidal reports that 43 percent of new uploads were completely AI-generated. On November 6, new uploads to Tidal hit a whopping 60 percent AI-generated. As things stand, Tidal hosts 27 million tracks labeled as AI, all of which were obviously added in the past couple of years. That accounts for 6.3 percent of Tidal's total catalog. On December 9, Tidal will delete all those songs. The streamer notes this will have essentially no negative impact because 96 percent of AI-labeled tracks got zero plays in the past 90 days. Throughout its announcement, Tidal is careful to stipulate that it's only talking about music that has been fully created by AI. Artists can still use AI tools as long as the final product contains human elements. Read full article Comments

title: Porsche 718 Boxster prototype drive: This electric roadster is real
author: Tim Stevens
body: Porsche provided flights from Albany, New York, to Los Angeles and accommodation so Ars could drive the 718 EV prototype. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. It wasn't until I was stuck in traffic on the way back from a run up and down some canyon roads that I realized just how low Porsche's upcoming all-electric 718 Boxster truly is. I was idly looking around at the other cars, doing the math on the EV adoption rate in this small sample of Los Angeles gridlock (roughly 50 percent, impressively) when I noticed that I was eye-level with a Tesla Model Y door handle. That's not particularly low for a sports car, but it's practically unheard of for an EV. Nearly all modern electric cars are built atop a skateboard-style battery pack, a stack of cells that elevates the seating position by a good 3 inches. In these SUV-heady days, that's usually not a problem, possibly even an advantage. But, in a car like this, the closer you can get your keister to the road, the greater the sensation of speed. So, for the company's first all-electric sports car, the 718 Boxster that will be fully revealed next year, Porsche engineers put the battery pack behind the driver. That powers a single motor spinning the rear wheels and creates a driving experience that both honors the simple joy of motoring in a mid-engined Boxster while pushing the 718 to new heights of power and performance. title: NASA may get $2 billion boost as White House seeks to accelerate Artemis
author: Eric Berger
body: As part of ongoing wrangling over the US budget for the current fiscal year, the White House on Monday night sent a list of budget exceptions to Congress that it seeks in the near term for the federal government ( PDF ). The list of so-called "funding anomalies" is dominated largely by appropriations for the Department of Defense, including the Golden Dome missile defense program championed by the Trump administration. However, among the highest non-defense exceptions is $2 billion for NASA's Artemis program for a "higher rate of operations." The funding represents a significant 25 percent boost for NASA's Artemis program, which received approximately $7.8 billion in fiscal year 2026. Technically, the White House is seeking to increase the annualized funding rate for Artemis to $9.8 billion, rather than immediately providing NASA with an additional $2 billion. It comes at a time when it is increasingly clear that China's lunar ambitions are as expansive as NASA's, and there is a good chance the country reaches the Moon with astronauts before NASA can get back there. title: Homo erectus lived in the rainforest alongside Denisovans
author: Kiona N. Smith
body: Homo erectus was walking around mainland Asia at least 60,000 years more recently than archaeologists thought. A handful of teeth from two caves in southern China's Guangxi Province just filled in a significant gap in the fossil record of a region that's vital to the story of how our genus, Homo , took over the world. The chemical makeup of the teeth's enamel suggests that, over the course of their lives, these Homo erectus moved across surprisingly large distances and made their living in dense tropical rainforests—an environment we'd previously assumed that only our species had ever gained a real foothold in. And one of the teeth offers a strong clue that Homo erectus probably shared this vast landscape with the Denisovans. A handful of teeth with a lot to say Baxian and Naxian are a pair of limestone caves that lie 15 kilometers apart along a karst valley corridor in southern China. University of Copenhagen paleoanthropologist Frido Welker and his colleagues unearthed a total of nine hominin teeth from among the more than 18,000 bones and fragments from non-hominin animals found there. Macquarie University paleoanthropologist Kira Westaway and her colleagues analyzed proteins and chemical isotopes from the enamel of five of these teeth. Read full article Comments

Huang was visibly moved as one colleague threw themselves into his arms for a hug. The spectacular reinstatement of the chief executive of Nvidia, less than two weeks after he resigned in a scandal over an affair with a customer and suspected Chinese spy—as well as a second reported affair with a subordinate—caught even the company’s most senior executives by surprise. The abrupt reversal by Nvidia’s board was spurred by President Donald Trump, who applied pressure to the board over the weekend after watching what was once America’s most valuable company as well as the wider tech sector haemorrhage value last week. title: Amazon says hackers' AI agents found and exploited 0-day with little human input
author: Dan Goodin
body: Amazon said AI agents recently found and exploited a zero-day vulnerability with no human oversight beyond a simple instruction to get root access on an East Asian university server. The agents were running on Cairn, an open source AI penetration-testing framework. The hackers, who provided prompts in simplified Chinese and configured the model to the Chinese Standard Time zone, gave the agents a list of IP addresses and the goal: “obtain shell access.” In short order, the agents discovered a zero-day in an open source medical imaging AI application running on one of the target servers. The agents then exploited the vulnerability and gained full control of the system. “These findings show that agentic offensive operations are already happening, and defenders should prepare for the speed and persistence these tools enable,” Amazon said . title: Ukraine sinks Russian warship, strikes cargo ships from Mediterranean to Baltic
author: Jeremy Hsu
body: Ukrainian explosive naval drones sank a Russian warship docked in the port city of Benghazi in Libya while also striking a Russian cargo ship that it was escorting. The incident demonstrates the expanding scope of Ukrainian military strikes on Russian ships from the coast of North Africa to the Gulf of Finland. The Russian Navy’s missile corvette Merkury sank at port after being struck by at least two Ukrainian naval drones on November 22, according to The Associated Press . Ukraine’s Security Service described using seven naval drones launched from a mother ship to target the Merkury , and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy shared video footage showing the drone boats approaching and exploding against both the burning Russian warship and a Russian dry cargo ship, MV Angara . Zelenskyy noted that a Ka-27 combat helicopter onboard the Merkury was also destroyed. He described the cargo ship MV Angara as transporting weapons—Russia provides material support to the Libyan National Army that currently controls Benghazi and is battling the internationally recognized Libyan government based in Tripoli. body: Nvidia has reinstated co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO less than two weeks after he stepped down, and less than a week after the company's board said it had no intention of bringing him back . Reactions to Huang's return have been a mix of praise, criticism, and jokes, with several other tech executives rallying around him. SEE ALSO: Nvidia's board reinstates Jensen Huang as CEO following Trump's endorsement Nvidia announced Huang's resignation on Nov. 12 , a day after the board accepted it with immediate effect. He stepped down amid reports that he'd had extramarital affairs with both an alleged Chinese spy and a Nvidia employee , with allegations of a third affair with another worker subsequently surfacing. His relationship with Alice Huang (no relation) drew particular scrutiny, as she was suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips. She previously led Megaspeed, a company U.S. authorities have been investigating over concerns it smuggled advanced Nvidia chips to China in circumvention of U.S. restrictions . While Huang said that he would be "honored" to return as CEO if asked, the board stated said on Nov. 17 that it did not plan to bring him back . Yet after reported pressure from President Donald Trump , the chipmaker has put Huang back in the top job after all. In a press release announcing Huang's reinstatement, Nvidia stated that it had based the decision on "input from senior levels of the United States government." body: Fully autonomous cyberattacks are here, according to Google and its cybersecurity firm Mandiant. The Google Threat Intelligence Group recently released a report revealing that cyberattackers are now using multi-agent AI frameworks capable of searching for vulnerabilities and exploiting them independently. Furthermore, these tactics are already being used in cyberattack campaigns. Google cybersecurity researchers uncovered "an exposed staging server hosting a multi-agent vulnerability research and weaponization framework dubbed exploit_agent," which "integrates with multiple frontier and local LLMs." Google's investigation revealed that the entity behind the server hosting this framework appeared to be specifically targeting French websites in the media and entertainment sector. Some education sites were targeted as well. Google's report cites even more examples of fully autonomous cyberattacks. In one example, the cybersecurity firm Greynoise found that a bad actor used LLMs to identify vulnerabilities and automatically build exploits. The hacker was able to put together a list of targets and then execute the exploits against hundreds of organizations. In one particular hack, the threat actor was able to gain administrator access "within minutes." The adversary went from an empty workspace to first achieving RCE against a real victim in just under four hours, first domain admin in an additional two hours, and once the full campaign launched, compromised at least 11 organizations in 26 seconds. title: What does Dig co-creator Mike Schur think of Parks and Recreation comparisons?
body: Right from the moment Peacock's Dig was announced, comparisons to Parks and Recreation felt inevitable. The new sitcom reunites Parks and Recreation 's co-creator Mike Schur with the show's leading lady, Amy Poehler . As co-creators on Dig, the two once more deliver a workplace comedy about a competent, passionate leader, played by Poehler, who assembles a motley team. In Dig 's case, that's archaeologist Elise, who's overseeing a Grecian archaeological dig site. "When we started Parks and Rec , we were compared to The Office , because The Office was such a big deal at the time," Schur told Mashable over Zoom. "That was sort of our mini obstacle we had to get through." Both shows were workplace-set mockumentaries on NBC. Critics and viewers alike were quick to call out the similarities. While talking with Steve Carell for an episode of Good Hang earlier this year, Poehler recalled , " Parks and Rec had the worst launch ever. Everyone was like, 'This is not The Office . We don't like this.'" However, Parks and Recreation ditched Office -like cynicism in favor of a warmer tone, and it carved out a niche of its own. Still, for Schur, comparisons to The Office prepared him for how people might react to his later work. That includes Dig. title: Dig pulls off a perfect Parks and Rec reunion
body: Peacock's Dig is just one Parks and Recreation reunion after another. The archaeological comedy is co-created by Amy Poehler and Mike Schur, who both worked together on Parks and Recreation . Schur co-created that series with Greg Daniels, and Poehler led the show as waffle-loving civil servant Leslie Knope. SEE ALSO: 'Dig' review: Amy Poehler and 'Parks and Rec's Mike Schur have done it again However, Poehler and Schur's collaboration isn't the only spark of Parks and Recreation magic you'll find in Dig . In a blink-and-you'll-miss-it moment, Dig also features a cameo from none other than Rashida Jones, who plays Leslie's best friend, nurse Ann Perkins, in Parks and Recreation . Jones' appearance occurs in episode 5, when she pops up as a woman taking a photo of archaeologists Elise (Poehler) and Neville (Hugh Laurie) at a beachside restaurant. My Parks -loving self has never rewound a scene so fast to make sure my eyes weren't deceiving me. According to Schur, the cameo came about due to proximity. Dig shot in Italy and Greece, and Jones is semi-permanently located in London. Schur, Poehler, and Jones, who have been friends since even before working together on Parks and Recreation , were communicating with one another during production. title: U.S. intelligence chief says more tech outages are inevitably coming
body: Over the past month, tech outages have disrupted work emails, delayed bank transactions, and temporarily grounded departing flights across the United States. Most of the biggest disruptions happened within six days of one another. On Sunday, Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said Americans should expect more disruptions like these, but not because of an incoming cyberattack ; rather, because companies and government agencies are now in the process of updating aging technology. "We are going to have glitches, gaps, interruptions in service," Clayton told CNN's State of the Union on Sunday, Nov. 24. "That is going to happen." He said much of the country's digital infrastructure was built over three decades or more and needs upgrades to run better and stay secure. (As one example, the FAA is still in the process of phasing out floppy disks , with a target of retiring the '90s-era technology by 2028.) Clayton compared it to weekend maintenance at work: A company might take a system offline on Saturday and plan to have it back by 2 A.M. Sunday. If the team finds another problem during the upgrade, it might be Sunday afternoon before the system is back up. "We are taking more systems down and putting them back up than ever before," he said. SEE ALSO: Are the recent outages connected? What we know. It was a lot to keep track of in six days: On Nov. 12, some Microsoft Outlook users couldn't open their inboxes or send email. title: Trump halts Iowa detonation, says new governor to blame if it blows accidentally
author: Beth Mole
body: President Trump took to social media Monday afternoon to announce that he has ordered the US military to halt plans to detonate 68 deteriorating barrels of lead azide at an Army ammunition plant in Middletown, Iowa. Trump claimed that the fate of the unstable, highly explosive material is now in the hands of a federal court and Rob Sand, Iowa's governor-elect, who won't be sworn into office until January. The Army had planned to detonate the barrels on November 20, but delayed the blast on Thursday amid public outcry and a legal challenge from environmental groups. The explosion will launch a plume of toxic gases and neurotoxic lead that could reach up to 100 miles away from the Iowa facility, the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP). Iowa residents and officials said they learned of the detonation only days beforehand. The environmental groups, led by Earthjustice, claimed in an emergency court filing that the Army had not fully considered safer options for disposing of the lead azide before planning the detonation. body: On Monday, Virginia and Oregon became the first states to sue SpaceX, alleging that Grok continues to sexualize, unchecked, real photos of mostly women and children. SpaceX acquired xAI in February and now must handle the ongoing reckoning over the controversial rollout of Grok’s “spicy mode”—a model feature Musk hyped but was soon found to generate a flood of non-consensual intimate imagery (NCII) and child sex abuse images (CSAM). Initial safeguards were so lax that Grok sometimes generated nude images without being asked . Although X Safety and xAI (now known as SpaceXSI) were silent at first , Musk’s companies eventually apologized and claimed that additional safeguards were implemented and policies redesigned to block harmful outputs. However, state attorneys general alleged that those statements were “misleading” and that SpaceXSI instead quietly “embraced” sexualized content to seize more AI market share, as Grok continues to generate NCII and CSAM today.
